# UNIT 8: Character, Society & Family (Akhlaq & Mu'amalat)
## Student Handout (Age 10)
---
*“Verily, I was sent only to perfect noble character.”* — Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him)

---

### Welcome, Young Scholar!
Welcome to your student guide for Unit 8. In this unit, we will explore how a Muslim is supposed to behave with others. We will look at what it means to be honest, how to stay humble, and how to control our anger. We will also learn about the rights of our parents, our family, and our neighbors, and how to choose good friends, navigate peer pressure, and understand justice.

We will learn these topics through the teachings of the **Maliki school** of Islamic law (*fiqh*) and the **Ash'ari school** of Islamic belief (*aqidah*). 

As you read, you will see special terms in bold. These are Arabic words that scholars use. Make sure you learn their meanings!

---

## Page 2: Creed Connect — Why Do We Choose Goodness?

Before we look at manners, we have to ask an important question: **Why do we do good deeds?** In our creed (*aqidah*), we learn two very special rules that explain this.

### 1. Good and Bad are Defined by Allah (Al-Husn wal-Qubh)
In the **Ash'ari** school of belief, we believe that we know what is good and what is bad because Allah told us in the Quran and through the Prophet (pbuh). This is called **Al-Husn wal-Qubh** (الْحُسْن وَالْقُبْح – Goodness and Badness). 
*   Why is honesty good? It is not just because people like it; it is because **Allah commanded it**.
*   Why is lying bad? It is because **Allah forbade it**.
*   Our minds can see that some things are helpful, but only Allah's law (*Al-Shar'*) decides what is truly a good deed that earns rewards in Jannah.

### 2. We Choose, and Allah Creates (Kasb)
Have you ever wondered: *Does Allah make me do good, or do I do it myself?*
*   Our creed teaches the concept of **Kasb** (كَسْب – Acquisition). 
*   Allah is the Creator (*Khaliq*) of everything, including our actions.
*   But Allah gave us a choice. When you decide in your heart to help your mom or tell the truth, you are "choosing" (*Kasb*) that action. Because you chose it, Allah creates the action for you, and He rewards you for your good choice!

> **Creed Focus Box: My Choice matters!**
> Since we choose (*Kasb*) our actions, we are fully responsible for our manners. We cannot say, *"I have a bad temper because Allah made me this way."* We must choose to be patient and polite!

---

## Page 3: The Three Jewels of Personal Character

Let's look at three powerful qualities that every young Muslim should wear like beautiful jewels.

### 1. Honesty (Sidq)
**Sidq** (صِدْق) means truthfulness and sincerity. The Prophet (pbuh) said that truthfulness leads us to goodness, and goodness leads to Jannah. 
To practice *Sidq*, we must be honest in three ways:
*   **Honest Words:** We never tell lies, even when we are joking or trying to get out of trouble.
*   **Honest Actions:** We do what we say. We don't pretend to be good when adults are watching and then act differently when they leave.
*   **Honest Intentions:** We do good things only to make Allah happy, not to show off.

### 2. Humility (Tawadu')
**Tawadu'** (تَوَاضُع) is humility. It means knowing that everything good about you—your smart brain, your athletic skills, your nice toys—is a gift from Allah. 
*   The opposite of humility is **Kibr** (كِبْر – Pride). Pride is looking down on others or refusing to accept the truth when you are wrong.
*   A humble person is kind to everyone, helps wash the dishes, and never brags about being better than others.

### 3. Controlling Anger (Kadhm al-Ghaydh)
Anger is like a hot spark from Shaytan. The Prophet (pbuh) taught us that a strong person is not someone who wins a physical fight, but someone who can control themselves when angry.
*   **Kadhm al-Ghaydh** (كَظْم الْغَيْظ) means locking up your anger inside and choosing to react with peace.
*   **Hilm** (حِلْم) is gentleness and patience that we build over time.

---

## Page 4: Character in the Law — What is Muru'ah?

In Islam, good character is not just a suggestion; it has real legal importance. In the **Maliki school of law**, there is a special concept called **Muru'ah**.

### What is Muru'ah?
**Muru'ah** (مُرُوءَة) translates to **chivalry, dignity, and honorable behavior**. It means acting in a way that is polite, respectful of others, and noble.

### How does Muru'ah affect us legally?
In an Islamic court of law, if someone wants to testify as a witness, the judge (*Qadi*) must check if they are an upright person. This quality is called **'Adalah** (عَدَالَة).
*   If a person lacks **Muru'ah**, they lose their **'Adalah**, and the judge will **reject their testimony**!
*   **What destroys Muru'ah for a 10-year-old?**
    *   Screaming and throwing temper tantrums in public.
    *   Playing mean or dangerous pranks on others.
    *   Lying to teachers or friends, even as a joke.
    *   Using bad language or acting foolishly for attention.

> **Law Check Box: The Dignified Muslim**
> Imam Malik taught that a Muslim should always carry themselves with quiet dignity. When we behave rudely, we are not just being impolite; we are showing that we cannot be trusted with important matters in our community.

---

## Page 5: My First Circle — Parents & Family

Our family is the most important group of people in our lives. Allah has given them special rights over us.

### 1. Loving and Obeying Parents (Birr al-Walidayn)
Allah says in the Quran that we must worship Him alone, and right after that, He commands us to show **Birr al-Walidayn** (بِرّ الْوَالِدَيْن – Righteous treatment of parents).
*   **No "Uff"!** Allah tells us in Surah al-Isra not to say even a small sigh of frustration, like *"Uff"* (أُفّ) or *"Argh!"*, when they ask us to do something.
*   **Obedience:** We must obey our parents in everything that is permissible (like cleaning our room, doing homework, or eating healthy food). The only time we do not obey them is if they command us to do something against Allah's law (like skipping Salah). But even then, we must speak to them with extreme kindness and love.

### 2. Legal Duty to Parents (Nafaqah)
In the Maliki school, when parents grow old and if they become poor, it is a **strict legal obligation** on their adult children to pay for their food, clothing, and home. This is called **Nafaqah** (نَفَقَة – Maintenance).

### 3. Connecting with Family (Silat al-Rahim)
**Silat al-Rahim** (صِلَة الرَّحِم) means connecting with your blood relatives (grandparents, aunts, uncles, cousins). 
*   The word *Rahim* means womb, showing that we are tied together by birth.
*   Cutting off family ties (*Qat' al-Rahim*) is a major sin. We must visit, call, or send cards to our relatives to keep our love alive!

---

## Page 6: My Neighbors — The 40-House Rule

Who is your neighbor? Is it just the family living next door? 

### The Maliki Definition of a Neighbor
According to **Imam Malik**, your neighbors are not just the people directly next to you. The neighborhood extends to **forty (40) houses in every direction**—in front, behind, to the left, and to the right! 

```
                    40 Houses North
                          ^
                          |
40 Houses West <--- [ YOUR HOUSE ] ---> 40 Houses East
                          |
                          v
                    40 Houses South
```

### The Rights of Neighbors (Huquq al-Jiwar)
Having neighbors means we must respect **Huquq al-Jiwar** (حُقُوق الْجِوَار – Rights of the Neighborhood). The Prophet (pbuh) said: *"Angel Jibril kept advising me to treat neighbors kindly until I thought he would make them my heirs."*

*   **Do Not Harm Them:** Never make loud noises that keep them awake, dump trash near their property, or let pets ruin their gardens.
*   **Be Generous:** The Prophet (pbuh) said that if you cook a warm soup, you should add extra water so you can share a bowl with your neighbor!
*   **Maliki Law on Neighbor Harm:** In our school, if a person does something on their own property that causes real harm to a neighbor (like blocking their light or window views), a judge can legally force them to change it.

---

## Page 7: True Friends vs. Peer Pressure

The friends you spend time with have a massive impact on who you become. 

### The Perfume Seller and the Blacksmith
The Prophet (pbuh) gave a beautiful example of friendship:
*   **The Good Friend** is like a perfume seller (**Misk**). Even if you don't buy any perfume, just standing near them makes you smell nice!
*   **The Bad Friend** is like a blacksmith working with fire. The sparks might burn your clothes, or at least you will walk away smelling like smoke.

### What is Peer Pressure?
Peer pressure is when friends try to push you to do things you know are wrong—like cheating on a test, skipping prayers, or being mean to someone. 
*   **The Khalil Rule:** The Prophet (pbuh) said: *"A person is on the religion of his close friend (*Khalil*), so let each of you look to whom he takes as a close friend."*
*   **Standing Strong:** A Muslim with **Muru'ah** (dignity) has the strength to say *"No"* when friends do bad things. If they don't stop, a true Muslim walks away and finds better company (**Suhbah Salihah** – Righteous companionship).

> **Maliki Court Rule: Friendship & Bias**
> In the Maliki school, if you are extremely close friends with someone, you cannot testify in court *in favor* of them. The law knows that your love for your friend might make it hard for you to be completely unbiased! This shows how powerful friendship is.

---

## Page 8: The Digital Screen — Social Media with a Clean Heart

Even though phones and tablets are fun, they present new challenges to our character. We must use them with an Islamic mindset.

### Protecting the Five Necessities (Al-Daruriyyat al-Khams)
Islamic law is designed to protect five important things: **Religion, Life, Intellect, Honor, and Wealth**. Social media can easily harm two of these:

1.  **Guarding the Intellect (*Hifdh al-'Aql*):** Doom-scrolling (watching short videos for hours) makes our brains tired and distracts us from Salah and schoolwork. We must control our screen time.
2.  **Guarding Honor (*Hifdh al-'Ird*):** It is very easy to write mean comments, share secrets, or make fun of people online. In Islam, guarding a person's honor (**'Ird** / عِرْض) is sacred.

### Maliki Rule: Sadd al-Dhara'i' (Blocking the Paths to Harm)
In the Maliki school, there is a legal rule called **Sadd al-Dhara'i'** (سَدّ الذَّرَائِع). It means: **"If something leads to sin, we must block it before the sin happens."**
*   If a certain video app always leads you to hear bad language or waste hours of time, the rule of *Sadd al-Dhara'i'* suggests you should delete it or set a strict limit.
*   If a group chat is full of gossip (*Gheebah*), you should leave it immediately.

---

## Page 9: Justice & Fairness — The Scales of Life

Islam teaches us to be fair to everyone, not just our friends or people we like.

### 1. Justice ('Adl) and Equity (Qist)
*   **'Adl** (عَدْل) means justice and giving everyone their rights.
*   **Qist** (قِسْط) means equity or fairness in how we treat people daily.
*   Allah says in the Quran: *"Be just! That is closer to piety."* (Surah al-Ma'idah: 8). We must be fair even if we are testifying against ourselves or our families.

### 2. Oppression (Zulm) is Haram
Oppression is called **Zulm** (ظُلْم). It means taking away someone's rights or treating them cruelly. Allah says in a Hadith Qudsi: *"I have forbidden oppression for Myself, and I have made it forbidden among you, so do not oppress one another."*

### 3. Serving the Public Interest (Maslahah Mursalah)
In Maliki fiqh, when there is no direct rule in the Quran about a modern problem, scholars use **Maslahah Mursalah** (مَصْلَحَة مُرْسَلَة) – the rule of **Public Interest**—to make decisions.
*   This means we support rules that keep people safe (like speed limits, school guidelines, and playground safety).
*   A good Muslim always acts in a way that brings benefit to the community and prevents harm.

---

## Page 10: Reflection Corner & Sources

### Short Reflection Question (Critical Thinking)
> **Reflect and Write:** 
> Imagine you are playing an online multiplayer video game with your friends. One friend starts using bad language and cyberbullying a new player. The other friends in the chat start laughing and joining in. 
> 
> 1. How does the Maliki concept of **Muru'ah** (dignity) apply to how you behave in this situation? 
> 2. How can you use the principle of **Sadd al-Dhara'i'** (blocking the path to harm) to protect your own heart and mind (*'Aql*) here? Write a short plan (3-4 sentences) of what you would do.

***

### Bibliography of Sources
Here are the classic books of Islamic knowledge that we used to build this guide:
1.  **Imam Malik ibn Anas**, *Al-Muwatta* — The oldest collection of Hadith and rulings from the city of Madinah.
2.  **Ibn Abi Zayd al-Qayrawani**, *Al-Risalah* — A famous Maliki manual written over 1,000 years ago for students.
3.  **Imam al-Ghazali**, *Ihya 'Ulum al-Din* (Revival of the Religious Sciences) — The ultimate guide to inner character (*Akhlaq*) and humility.
4.  **Imam al-Sanusi**, *Al-Aqidah al-Sanusiyyah* — The standard book of Ash'ari theology.

# Assessment Questions: Character, Society & Family
## For Student Handout (Age 10)
---

### Part A: Multiple Choice (10 Questions)
*Select the best answer for each question.*

1.  **What does the Ash'ari creed teach us about Al-Husn wal-Qubh (Goodness and Badness)?**
    *   a) Our own brains are the only things that decide what makes an action rewardable.
    *   b) Goodness and badness of actions are determined by Allah's commands and laws.
    *   c) Good and bad change depending on our mood.
    *   d) There is no such thing as good and bad actions.

2.  **What is the meaning of the theological term Kasb (Acquisition)?**
    *   a) Allah is the Creator of all actions, but we choose our intentions and actions.
    *   b) We create our own actions without Allah's help.
    *   c) Everything is forced upon us, and we have no choice.
    *   d) Making money in the marketplace.

3.  **What is the Arabic word for truthfulness and sincerity in speech, action, and intention?**
    *   a) *Tawadu'*
    *   b) *Muru'ah*
    *   c) *Sidq*
    *   d) *Qist*

4.  **How is Kibr (Pride) defined in Islamic teachings?**
    *   a) Being happy with your new clothes.
    *   b) Rejecting the truth and looking down on other people.
    *   c) Being shy around strangers.
    *   d) Helping your family clean the house.

5.  **Which of these is the first step recommended by the Prophet (pbuh) when you feel Ghadab (anger)?**
    *   a) Shout as loud as you can to release the stress.
    *   b) Say *A'udhu billahi min ash-Shaytan ir-Rajeem* (Seek refuge in Allah from Shaytan).
    *   c) Run around the block.
    *   d) Ignore the person forever.

6.  **In the Maliki school, what is Muru'ah?**
    *   a) Performing the Wudu rubbing obligation.
    *   b) Chivalry, dignity, and honorable public behavior.
    *   c) Paying money to poor relatives.
    *   d) Wiping the entire head.

7.  **If a person lacks Muru'ah in Maliki fiqh, what is the legal consequence?**
    *   a) They must pay a fine to the mosque.
    *   b) They must repeat their prayers.
    *   c) Their testimony as a witness in court is rejected.
    *   d) They are not allowed to travel.

8.  **According to Imam Malik, how far does your neighborhood extend for Huquq al-Jiwar (neighborhood rights)?**
    *   a) Just the houses next door to you.
    *   b) 7 houses in every direction.
    *   c) 40 houses in every direction.
    *   d) The entire city.

9.  **What does the Maliki legal concept Sadd al-Dhara'i' mean?**
    *   a) Helping a friend cheat.
    *   b) Blocking the pathways that lead to sin before the sin happens.
    *   c) Sharing food with neighbors.
    *   d) Respecting your grandparents.

10. **In Islamic law, which of these is NOT one of the five essential things protected by the Shariah?**
    *   a) Religion (*Din*)
    *   b) Intellect (*'Aql*)
    *   c) Video game high scores
    *   d) Honor (*'Ird*)

---

### Part B: Scenario-Based Questions (5 Questions)
*Read the scenario and write or choose the correct response based on the curriculum.*

11. **Yunus wants to play a voluntary online game tournament that takes all weekend, but his parents ask him to stay home and help look after his younger siblings. He thinks, "This is voluntary, so I can just go anyway." What is the Maliki ruling on this?**
    *   *Answer:* Yunus is incorrect. In Maliki fiqh, parental permission is required for voluntary travel or voluntary undertakings that affect the parents. Serving his parents and showing them **Birr al-Walidayn** (righteous treatment) is a strict obligation (*Wajib*), which takes priority over voluntary activities.

12. **Layla is in a WhatsApp group chat with her classmates. Two girls start sharing private messages from another classmate to make fun of her. Layla doesn't write anything bad, but she keeps reading the messages. How can Layla use Sadd al-Dhara'i' here?**
    *   *Answer:* Layla should apply **Sadd al-Dhara'i'** (blocking the path to harm) by leaving the group chat. Even though she isn't typing bad comments, staying in the chat makes her a silent witness to gossiping (*Gheebah*) and violates the duty of guarding honor (**Hifdh al-'Ird**). Leaving the chat blocks the path to participating in the sin.

13. **Zayd is building a treehouse in his backyard. He wants to build a large window that points directly into his neighbor's bedroom window. Can his neighbor complain, and what is the Maliki legal view?**
    *   *Answer:* Yes, the neighbor can complain. In Maliki law, there is a rule of **Da'f al-Darar** (prevention of harm). A property owner is legally blocked from using their property in a way that causes direct harm or violates the privacy of their neighbor. Zayd would be forced to block or move the window.

14. **Amina is extremely close friends with Salma. They share everything and are best friends. Salma is involved in a small dispute at school, and the principal asks Amina to give witness testimony. In a Maliki court of law, would Amina's testimony in favor of Salma be accepted?**
    *   *Answer:* No. In the Maliki school, testimony in favor of an intimate close friend (**Shahadat al-Sadiq li-Sadiqihi**) is rejected because the legal system recognizes that the bond of friendship is so strong that it can create bias, making it hard to be objective.

15. **Hamzah drops his tablet and cracks the screen. He gets very angry, screams, and throws his toy across the room. His older brother tells him to think about Qadar (Divine Decree). How does this help?**
    *   *Answer:* Believing in **Qadar** means knowing that the tablet cracking was already decreed by Allah as a test. Knowing that everything is in Allah's hands helps Hamzah accept the situation, remain patient (*Sabr*), and immediately cool down his anger (*Kadhm al-Ghaydh*).

---

### Part C: Short Answer & Matching (5 Questions)
*Answer the questions briefly or match the terms.*

16. **Match the Arabic term to its correct definition:**
    *   1. *Tawadu'*  --> ______ (Answer: Humility/Knowing blessings are from Allah)
    *   2. *'Adl*      --> ______ (Answer: Justice/Putting things in their proper place)
    *   3. *'Ird*      --> ______ (Answer: Personal honor and dignity)
    *   4. *Nafaqah*   --> ______ (Answer: Legal obligation to financially maintain poor parents)

17. **What did the Prophet (pbuh) mean when he said a good friend is like a perfume seller (Misk)?**
    *   *Answer:* He meant that good company (*Suhbah Salihah*) naturally influences you in a positive way. Even if they don't teach you directly, just being around them makes your character and actions better.

18. **Why does Allah forbid saying even "Uff" (أُفّ) to parents?**
    *   *Answer:* Because "Uff" is the smallest expression of irritation or annoyance. By forbidding even this tiny sound, Allah is teaching us that we must treat our parents with the utmost gentleness and respect, avoiding all forms of frustration toward them.

19. **What is the difference between 'Adl (justice) and Qist (equity)?**
    *   *Answer:* **'Adl** is giving everyone their exact rights under the law. **Qist** is fairness that takes into account the specific needs and situations of different people (like giving different sized shoes to people of different ages).

20. **Give one example of Maslahah Mursalah (Public Interest) that we follow in modern schools or cities.**
    *   *Answer:* School fire drills or wearing seatbelts in a car. These are modern rules that aren't mentioned in the Quran directly, but they protect human life and safety, which is a major goal of Islamic law.

12. **Layla is in a WhatsApp group chat with her classmates. Two girls start sharing private messages from another classmate to make fun of her. Layla doesn't write anything bad, but she keeps reading the messages. How can Layla use Sadd al-Dhara'i' here?**
    *   *Answer:* Layla should apply **Sadd al-Dhara'i'** (blocking the path to harm) by leaving the group chat. Even though she isn't typing bad comments, staying in the chat makes her a silent witness to gossiping (*Gheebah*) and violates the duty of guarding honor (**Hifdh al-'Ird**). Leaving the chat blocks the path to participating in the sin.

13. **Zayd is building a treehouse in his backyard. He wants to build a large window that points directly into his neighbor's bedroom window. Can his neighbor complain, and what is the Maliki legal view?**
    *   *Answer:* Yes, the neighbor can complain. In Maliki law, there is a rule of **Da'f al-Darar** (prevention of harm). A property owner is legally blocked from using their property in a way that causes direct harm or violates the privacy of their neighbor. Zayd would be forced to block or move the window.

14. **Amina is extremely close friends with Salma. They share everything and are best friends. Salma is involved in a small dispute at school, and the principal asks Amina to give witness testimony. In a Maliki court of law, would Amina's testimony in favor of Salma be accepted?**
    *   *Answer:* No. In the Maliki school, testimony in favor of an intimate close friend (**Shahadat al-Sadiq li-Sadiqihi**) is rejected because the legal system recognizes that the bond of friendship is so strong that it can create bias, making it hard to be objective.

15. **Hamzah drops his tablet and cracks the screen. He gets very angry, screams, and throws his toy across the room. His older brother tells him to think about Qadar (Divine Decree). How does this help?**
    *   *Answer:* Believing in **Qadar** means knowing that the tablet cracking was already decreed by Allah as a test. Knowing that everything is in Allah's hands helps Hamzah accept the situation, remain patient (*Sabr*), and immediately cool down his anger (*Kadhm al-Ghaydh*).

---

### Part C: Short Answer & Matching (5 Questions)
*Answer the questions briefly or match the terms.*

16. **Match the Arabic term to its correct definition:**
    *   1. *Tawadu'*  --> ______ (Answer: Humility/Knowing blessings are from Allah)
    *   2. *'Adl*      --> ______ (Answer: Justice/Putting things in their proper place)
    *   3. *'Ird*      --> ______ (Answer: Personal honor and dignity)
    *   4. *Nafaqah*   --> ______ (Answer: Legal obligation to financially maintain poor parents)

17. **What did the Prophet (pbuh) mean when he said a good friend is like a perfume seller (Misk)?**
    *   *Answer:* He meant that good company (*Suhbah Salihah*) naturally influences you in a positive way. Even if they don't teach you directly, just being around them makes your character and actions better.

18. **Why does Allah forbid saying even "Uff" (أُفّ) to parents?**
    *   *Answer:* Because "Uff" is the smallest expression of irritation or annoyance. By forbidding even this tiny sound, Allah is teaching us that we must treat our parents with the utmost gentleness and respect, avoiding all forms of frustration toward them.

19. **What is the difference between 'Adl (justice) and Qist (equity)?**
    *   *Answer:* **'Adl** is giving everyone their exact rights under the law. **Qist** is fairness that takes into account the specific needs and situations of different people (like giving different sized shoes to people of different ages).

20. **Give one example of Maslahah Mursalah (Public Interest) that we follow in modern schools or cities.**
    *   *Answer:* School fire drills or wearing seatbelts in a car. These are modern rules that aren't mentioned in the Quran directly, but they protect human life and safety, which is a major goal of Islamic law.

# UNIT 8: Character, Society & Family (Akhlaq & Mu'amalat)
## Student Handout (Age 13)
---
*“A person is on the religion of his close friend (khalil), so let each of you look to whom he takes as a close friend.”* — Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him)

---

### Introduction: Character, Community, and Jurisprudential Integrity
Welcome to your study guide for Unit 8. As an early teen, you are navigating complex social environments, peer dynamics, and digital spaces. This unit is designed to bridge the gap between abstract moral theories and real-world application. We will study the rules of character (*Akhlaq*) and social interactions (*Mu'amalat*) through two systematic frameworks:
1.  **Ash'ari Creed (Aqidah):** The theological framework that defines our relationship with God and explains the reality of human actions.
2.  **Maliki Jurisprudence (Fiqh):** The legal school founded by Imam Malik ibn Anas (d. 179 AH) in Madinah, which shows us how character translates into legal duties and community harmony.

As you go through this text, pay close attention to the bold Arabic legal and theological terms. Understanding these terms will help you build **fiqh literacy**—the ability to understand how Islamic law analyzes and resolves real-life ethical scenarios.

---

## Page 2: Theological Foundations — Divine Command Ethics & Kasb

To build a solid Islamic mindset, we must first establish the theological basis for morality. Why is something "good" or "bad"? How do our choices interact with God's power? The Ash'ari school of creed provides clear answers.

### 1. Divine Command Ethics (Al-Husn wal-Qubh al-Shar'iyyan)
In Ash'ari theology, moral values are not defined by subjective human utility or pure intellect. Instead, they are defined by Divine revelation. This is known as the principle of **Al-Husn wal-Qubh al-Shar'iyyan** (الْحُسْن وَالْقُبْح الشَّرْعِيَّان – Goodness and Badness are determined by the Law).
*   **The Limit of Reason (*'Aql*):** The human intellect can recognize that truthfulness is generally beneficial and lying is harmful. However, the intellect alone *cannot* determine whether an action is spiritually rewardable (*Thawab*) or punishable (*'Iqab*). 
*   **Revelation as the Standard:** We know honesty is a virtue and injustice is a vice because **Allah commanded the former and forbade the latter**. 
*   **Implication:** When you tell the truth, your intention should not merely be "it's the polite thing to do," but rather, "I am obeying a direct command of my Creator." This transforms daily ethics into active worship (*'Ibadah*).

### 2. The Concept of Acquisition (Kasb)
A key question in creed is how human choice interacts with Divine power:
*   We believe that Allah is the sole Creator (*Khaliq*) of all that exists, including human actions. 
*   However, human beings are given a free choice and the capacity to direct their intentions. When we resolve to perform an action, we "acquire" it. This is called **Kasb** (كَسْب – Acquisition).
*   Because we choose to acquire an action, we are morally responsible (*Mukallaf*) for it. Allah then creates the physical action in accordance with our choice. 

> **Creed Focus Box: Ethical Responsibility**
> The concept of *Kasb* prevents us from adopting fatalism (the belief that we have no choice and are forced to act). We choose our character traits; therefore, we are fully accountable before Allah for our temper, honesty, and treatment of others.

---

## Page 3: The Triad of Personal Ethics — Honesty, Humility, & Anger Control

Good character (*Akhlaq*) is built upon key virtues that govern our internal state and external actions. 

### 1. Honesty (Sidq)
**Sidq** (صِدْق) is truthfulness, but in Islamic ethics, it has three distinct dimensions:
*   **Truth in Speech (*Sidq al-Lisan*):** Absolute honesty in speech, avoiding lies, exaggerations, and deceptive half-truths, even in jest.
*   **Truth in Action (*Sidq al-'Amal*):** Consistency between one’s public actions and private state. Living without hypocrisy (*Nifaq*).
*   **Truth in Intention (*Sidq al-Niyyah*):** Directing all actions solely for the pleasure of Allah, free from the spiritual disease of showing off (*Riya'*).

### 2. Humility (Tawadu')
**Tawadu'** (تَوَاضُع) is the internal realization that all of your talents, intelligence, lineage, and wealth are blessings created and gifted by Allah, not achievements of your own ego.
*   The opposite is **Kibr** (كِبْر – Pride), which the Prophet (pbuh) defined as: *"Rejecting the truth and looking down on people."*
*   Humility requires us to accept correction when we make a mistake and to treat every person with respect, regardless of their social standing.

### 3. Anger Control (Kadhm al-Ghaydh) and Forbearance (Hilm)
Anger (*Ghadab*) is a destructive fire that disables the intellect (*'Aql*). 
*   **Kadhm al-Ghaydh** (كَظْم الْغَيْظ) is the immediate suppression of rage when one has the power to act on it.
*   **Hilm** (حِلْم) is the long-term cultivation of forbearance and emotional stability, rendering one slow to anger.
*   **Creed Link:** When we face provoking situations, recognizing **Qadar** (Divine Decree)—that this frustrating event has been permitted by Allah as a trial—allows us to respond with patience (*Sabr*) rather than rage.

---

## Page 4: Character and the Law — The Fiqh of Muru'ah (Dignity)

One of the best ways to build fiqh literacy is to understand how personal character impacts legal standing. In the **Maliki school of law**, manners are directly tied to judicial competence through the concept of **Muru'ah**.

### What is Muru'ah?
**Muru'ah** (مُرُوءَة) translates to **chivalry, dignity, and public honor**. It refers to behaving in a way that respects local customs (*'Urf*), maintains personal integrity, and avoids foolish or undignified behavior.

### The Legal Competence Connection ('Adalah)
In an Islamic court of law, for a judge (*Qadi*) to accept a witness's testimony, the witness must possess **'Adalah** (عَدَالَة – upright legal character). 
*   In Maliki fiqh, a person's **'Adalah** is compromised—and their testimony is **rejected**—if they lack **Muru'ah**!
*   **What destroys Muru'ah?**
    *   Behaving foolishly or screaming in public.
    *   Playing humiliating pranks on others for amusement.
    *   Dressing in a way that violates local norms of modesty and respect.
    *   Engaging in public behavior that suggests a lack of self-control or respect for others.

```
+-------------------------------------------------------+
|  Good Character (Akhlaq) -> Dignified Behavior (Muru'ah) |
|                          |                            |
|                          v                            |
|          Upright Legal Integrity ('Adalah)            |
|                          |                            |
|                          v                            |
|      Testimony Accepted in a Maliki Fiqh Court        |
+-------------------------------------------------------+
```

---

## Page 5: Filial Piety & Kinship — Spiritual Duties & Legal Obligations

The family is the foundational unit of Islamic society. The Shariah structures family relations with both spiritual recommendations and binding legal rules.

### 1. Filial Piety (Birr al-Walidayn)
Allah says: *"And your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him, and to parents, good treatment."* (Surah al-Isra: 23).
*   **The Spiritual Bond:** By pairing parents' rights directly with His own right to be worshiped, Allah shows the supreme status of parents. 
*   **The Limit of Annoyance:** The Quran forbids saying even *"Uff"* (أُفّ – a sigh of frustration or annoyance) to them. 

### 2. Legal Rulings in the Maliki School
*   **Parental Consent for Voluntary Travel:** In Maliki fiqh, if a child wishes to travel for voluntary acts (such as voluntary study abroad, voluntary travel, or voluntary military service), and the parents will suffer due to their absence or worry, the child **must** obtain their consent. Disobeying them in this is a sin.
*   **Financial Support (*Nafaqah* / نَفَقَة):** If parents become poor and are unable to earn a living, and their children have excess wealth, the children are **legally obligated** to provide financial support (food, shelter, clothing, medical care). This is a legal duty enforceable by a judge, not merely a voluntary charity.
*   **Witness Disqualification:** In Maliki law, children generally cannot testify *in favor* of their parents due to the high suspicion of natural bias (*Tuhmah*).

### 3. Family Ties (Silat al-Rahim)
**Silat al-Rahim** (صِلَة الرَّحِم) is the obligation to maintain ties with blood relatives. Severing these ties (*Qat' al-Rahim*) is a major sin. The true test of *Silat al-Rahim* is to connect with relatives who ignore or treat us poorly, acting solely for Allah's sake.

---

## Page 6: The Fiqh of Neighborhood — Spatial and Property Rights

Living in a community requires a clear definition of mutual rights. The Maliki school provides spatial boundaries and legal mechanisms to protect neighbor relations.

### 1. Spatial Definition of a Neighbor
How far does a neighborhood extend? In Maliki law, the neighborhood is defined as **forty (40) houses in every direction**: forty houses to the north, south, east, and west. This defines the immediate community that you must actively guard and support.

### 2. The Prohibition of Property Harm (Da'f al-Darar)
The Maliki school is exceptionally strict regarding neighborly harm, based on the Prophetic maxim: *"There shall be no harming nor reciprocating harm"* (*La darar wa la dirar*).
*   **Legal Restrictions on Property Use:** A homeowner cannot use their property in a way that causes direct harm to their neighbor. 
*   *Examples:* You cannot construct a high wall that blocks your neighbor’s existing window sunlight, install a window that overlooks their private family courtyard (violating their privacy), or build a chimney that directs smoke into their home. If you do, a Maliki judge will legally force you to modify or demolish the structure.

### 3. Right of Pre-emption (Shuf'ah)
**Shuf'ah** (شُفْعَة) is a legal right in Maliki fiqh where, if a person owns shared property (like a shared driveway, wall, or land) and wishes to sell their share, they **must** offer it to their partner/neighbor first. 
*   Only if the partner declines can they sell it to an outsider. 
*   This prevents a stranger who might cause harm or disruption from entering the neighborhood without the consent of the existing neighbors.

---

## Page 7: The Sociology of Companionship — Suhbah and the Law

Friendship in Islam is not just about entertainment; it is an active exchange of spiritual influence.

### 1. Spiritual Ecology of Friendship (Suhbah)
The Prophet (pbuh) warned: *"A person is on the religion of his close friend (*Khalil*), so let each of you look to whom he takes as a close friend."* 
*   **Suhbah Salihah** (صُحْبَة صَالِحَة) – Righteous companionship—acts as a protective shield. 
*   Conversely, bad company slowly desensitizes your heart to sin, just as sitting near a blacksmith's bellows eventually covers your clothes in smoke and ash.

### 2. The Legal Reality of Friendship in Maliki Fiqh
The Maliki school acknowledges the profound sociological influence of friendship by reflecting it in courtroom rules:
*   **Testimonial Disqualification (*Shahadat al-Sadiq li-Sadiqihi*):** If a person is called to testify in court, and the judge discovers that the witness is an intimate, close friend of the claimant, their testimony **in favor** of that friend is **rejected**.
*   **The Reason:** The law recognizes that close friendship (*Sadaqah*) creates a strong temptation to lie, cover up details, or show bias to protect one's friend.
*   **The Lesson:** True loyalty in Islam is to the truth and to Allah’s justice (*'Adl*), not to blind tribal or friendly allegiance.

```
                    Is the Witness an Intimate Friend?
                                  |
                 +----------------+----------------+
                 | Yes                             | No
                 v                                 v
   Testimony *in favor* is                    Testimony is evaluated
   disqualified due to bias.                  normally on its merits.
```

---

## Page 8: Navigating Peer Pressure & Social Media

Adolescence is defined by a desire for independence and belonging. However, we must view modern peer pressure and social media through an Islamic legal framework.

### 1. Guarding the Five Necessities (Al-Daruriyyat al-Khams)
Islamic law aims to protect five essential objectives (*Maqasid*): **Religion (*Din*), Life (*Nafs*), Intellect (*'Aql*), Honor (*'Ird*), and Wealth (*Mal*)**. Social media directly threatens two of these:
*   **Guarding the Intellect (*Hifdh al-'Aql*):** Mindless consumption of content destroys attention span, impairs critical thinking, and distracts from religious duties.
*   **Guarding Honor (*Hifdh al-'Ird* / حِفْظ الْعِرْض):** Guarding honor is a core duty. Social media makes it easy to engage in **Gheebah** (غِيبَة – Backbiting), **Namimah** (نَمِيمَة – Tale-bearing/spreading rumors), and **Tajassus** (تَجَسُّس – Spying/violating privacy). Sharing screenshots to humiliate someone is a direct violation of their *'Ird*.

### 2. Maliki Principle: Sadd al-Dhara'i' (Blocking the Means to Harm)
**Sadd al-Dhara'i'** (سَدّ الذَّرَائِع) is a foundational Maliki legal tool. It dictates that if a permissible action (*Mubah*) frequently leads to a forbidden result (*Haram*), that action itself must be restricted or blocked.
*   **Application:** If accessing a particular app or group chat consistently leads you to waste time, mock others, or view inappropriate material, you are legally encouraged (and sometimes obligated) to block, delete, or leave that space. You do not wait until you commit the major sin; you block the path beforehand.

---

## Page 9: Structural Justice & Equity

Justice in Islam is not merely personal; it is the structural goal of the entire legal system.

### 1. Justice ('Adl) vs. Equity (Qist)
*   **'Adl** (عَدْل) represents absolute justice and placing things in their proper place.
*   **Qist** (قِسْط) represents equity—ensuring fairness in practical application, adjusting for the specific needs and situations of individuals.
*   **Creed Detail:** In Ash'ari theology, Allah is Al-'Adl (The Just). Since He owns all of creation, whatever He decrees is just by definition. Oppression (*Zulm*) is impossible for Allah because He violates no one's rights—everything belongs to Him.

### 2. Oppression (Zulm)
**Zulm** (ظُلْم) means putting something in the wrong place or violating rights. It is strictly prohibited. The Prophet (pbuh) warned: *"Beware of oppression, for oppression will be darkness on the Day of Resurrection."*

### 3. Public Interest (Maslahah Mursalah)
**Maslahah Mursalah** (مَصْلَحَة مُرْسَلَة) is a key source of law in the Maliki school. It refers to general benefits that protect the community’s welfare but have no specific textual mention. 
*   **Example:** Copyright laws, data privacy acts, environmental regulations, and school honor codes. A Muslim respects these rules because they protect society (*Maslahah*). We actively work to be a source of benefit (*Naf'*) to those around us.

---

## Page 10: Advanced Reflection & Sources

### Short Reflection Question (Critical Engagement)
> **Ethical Case Study:**
> Farhan is a 13-year-old student who wants to join a popular online discord server run by his classmates. To get access, the moderator (his classmate) tells him he must share an embarrassing, private photo of another student as an "initiation prank." Farhan knows this photo will ruin that student's reputation at school.
> 
> 1. Analyze this scenario using the Maliki concept of **Muru'ah** (dignity) and the Islamic duty of guarding a person's **'Ird** (honor).
> 2. How can Farhan apply the Maliki legal principle of **Sadd al-Dhara'i'** (blocking the means to evil) to justify his refusal to join the server?
> 3. Provide a response (3-5 sentences) that Farhan can give to the moderator that demonstrates his commitment to justice (*'Adl*) without sounding self-righteous.

***

### Bibliography of Sources
1.  **Imam Malik ibn Anas**, *Al-Muwatta* — Classical collection of Hadith detailing the lived practice of Madinah.
2.  **Ibn Abi Zayd al-Qayrawani**, *Al-Risalah* — The foundational Maliki legal primer.
3.  **Imam al-Ghazali**, *Ihya 'Ulum al-Din* — Detailed spiritual analysis of pride (*Kibr*), humility (*Tawadu'*), and anger (*Ghadab*).
4.  **Imam Shihab al-Din al-Qarafi**, *Al-Furuq* — The premier Maliki work on legal philosophy, public interest (*Maslahah*), and blocking pathways to harm (*Sadd al-Dhara'i'*).
5.  **Imam al-Sanusi**, *Al-Aqidah al-Sanusiyyah* — The standard text on Ash'ari theological structures.

    *   *Answer:* Tariq should apply **Sadd al-Dhara'i'** (blocking the means to evil). The Maliki school holds that if a permissible action (using a chat app) frequently or inevitably leads to a forbidden result (seeing inappropriate content, desensitizing the heart to vulgarity), the means themselves must be blocked. This is due to **Tuhmah** (suspicion of bias), as the legal system recognizes that the bond of close friendship (*Sadaqah*) is highly likely to compromise objectivity and lead the witness to favor their friend over absolute justice (*'Adl*).

    *   *Answer:* **Muru'ah** refers to the dignity, chivalry, and noble behavior of an individual in alignment with local customs (*'Urf*). These compromise a person's *Muru'ah* because they demonstrate a lack of self-respect and emotional maturity. Legally, a person who lacks *Muru'ah* loses their **'Adalah** (legal integrity), and their testimony is rejected in a Maliki court.

    *   *Answer:* In Maliki fiqh, a neighbor is defined as someone living within **forty houses** in all four directions. These rules foster cohesion by preventing the intrusion of unwanted/harmful third parties into the local spatial community and ensuring that neighbors do not cause structural or privacy harm to one another, reducing social friction.

    *   *Answer:* Islam commands absolute justice (**'Adl**), even if it is against oneself, parents, or kin (Surah an-Nisa: 135).     *   *Answer:* **Maslahah Mursalah** allows the creation of rules that bring general benefit or prevent harm to society where there is no specific textual evidence. In the digital age, this principle can be applied to create rules such as screen-time limits, guidelines prohibiting the sharing of private chat screenshots (to protect honor/lineage, *Hifdh al-'Ird*), and rules against cyberbullying. # Presentation Slides: Character, Society & Family (Akhlaq & Mu'amalat)
## A Guide for Teachers (Maliki Fiqh & Ash'ari Aqidah)

---

# Slide 1: Welcome & Course Overview
## Character, Society & Family: The Outer Mirror of the Inner Soul
*   **Subject:** Islamic Studies (Akhlaq & Mu'amalat)
*   **Fiqh School:** Maliki (*Madhhab*)
*   **Creed School:** Ash'ari
*   **Core Focus:** Cultivating beautiful character (*Akhlaq*) internally and expressing it through just, legally sound interactions (*Mu'amalat*) with family, friends, and society.
*   **Key Themes:**
    *   Honesty, Humility, and Anger Management (*Sidq*, *Tawadu'*, *Kadhm al-Ghaydh*)
    *   Rights of Parents, Family, and Neighbors (*Birr al-Walidayn*, *Silat al-Rahim*, *Huquq al-Jiwar*)
    *   Choosing Friends and Navigating Peer Pressure (*Suhbah Salihah*)
    *   Social Media Ethics: Protecting Deen, Mind, and Honor
    *   Justice, Public Interest, and Legal Chivalry (*'Adl*, *Maslahah*, *Muru'ah*)

---
**Teacher Notes:**
*   **Welcome & Objective:** Welcome the students. Explain that this unit transitions from individual worship (*Taharah* and *Salah*) to social responsibility (*Mu'amalat*) and character development (*Akhlaq*).
*   **Pedagogical Note:** Highlight that we are studying these topics through the systematic framework of the **Maliki school of law** and the **Ash'ari school of creed**. Explain that character in Islam is not just an optional set of nice behaviors; it is deeply connected to theological truths and legal obligations.
*   **Discussion Starter:** Ask: *"Can a person have a perfect prayer (Salah) if they go home and treat their parents or neighbors poorly? Why is there a connection between worship and character?"*

---

# Slide 2: Creed Foundation: What Makes an Action "Good"?
## Divine Command Ethics (Al-Husn wal-Qubh al-Shar'iyyan)
*   **How do we know what is moral?**
    *   **Ash'ari Creed Ruling:** Moral goodness (*Al-Husn* / الْحُسْن) and moral badness (*Al-Qubh* / الْقُبْح) are determined directly by Allah's revelation (*Al-Shar'* / الشَّرْع).
*   **The Role of Reason (*'Aql*):**
    *   Human intellect can recognize that truth is useful or pain is bad.
    *   However, intellect alone *cannot* dictate what makes an action rewardable or punishable by Allah.
*   **Worship as Submission:**
    *   We tell the truth, honor parents, and act justly because **Allah commanded us to do so**. 
    *   Morality is not a human social contract; it is a response to Divine Command.

---
**Teacher Notes:**
*   **Ash'ari Theology Integration:** This slide introduces a core Ash'ari creed concept: *Al-Husn wal-Qubh al-Shar'iyyan* (Goodness and badness are defined by revelation). Contrast this briefly with the Mu'tazilite view (which held that reason alone can determine what is objectively good or bad in a way that binds Allah's judgment).
*   **Explanation:** Explain that for Ash'aris, if Allah commands something, it is good *because* He commanded it. If He forbids something, it is bad *because* He forbade it. 
*   **Example:** Helping the poor is good because Allah praised it and commanded it. If we only did it because it "felt nice," our reward would be worldly. When we do it because Allah commanded it, it becomes an act of worship (*'ibadah*).

---

# Slide 3: Perfecting Character: The Prophet’s Mission & Human Choice
## Understanding Character (Akhlaq) and Human Action (Kasb)
*   **The Prophetic Statement:** 
    *   The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: *"I was sent only to perfect noble character"* (*Innama bu'ithtu li-utammima makarim al-akhlaq*).
*   **Creed Connection: Acquisition (*Kasb* / كَسْب):**
    *   Allah is the Creator (*Khaliq*) of all actions, both good and bad.
    *   Human beings are the acquirers (*Muktasib*) of their actions.
    *   We use our free will to **choose** to act with honesty or anger, and Allah creates the physical action.
*   **Responsibility:**
    *   Because we choose to acquire the character traits, we are fully accountable (*Mukallaf*) before Allah for our choices.

---
**Teacher Notes:**
*   **Ash'ari Concept of Kasb:** Explain *Kasb* (acquisition) simply: Allah alone creates the ability and the action, but He gives humans the choice to direct their intention (*Niyyah*). When we choose to be patient, Allah creates the patience in us. Therefore, we cannot blame our bad temper on "how Allah made us"; we must choose to acquire good character.
*   **Hadith Citation:** The quote is recorded by Imam Malik in the *Muwatta* (Book of Good Character).
*   **Pedagogical Tip:** Emphasize that *Akhlaq* (plural of *Khuluq*) is not just passive personality; it is active choice and training of the soul (*Riyadat al-Nafs*).

---

# Slide 4: Honesty (Sidq): The Root of Trust
## Truthfulness in Word, Deed, and State
*   **What is Sidq?**
    *   **Sidq** (صِدْق) means truthfulness, sincerity, and consistency.
*   **Three Levels of Honesty:**
    1.  **Truth in Speech (*Sidq al-Lisan*):** Never telling lies, even in jest.
    2.  **Truth in Action (*Sidq al-'Amal*):** Making sure your outer actions match your inner intentions. No hypocrisy (*Nifaq*).
    3.  **Truth in Intention (*Sidq al-Niyyah*):** Doing good purely for the sake of Allah, not to show off (*Riya'*).
*   **The Ultimate Status:**
    *   The Prophet (pbuh) said: *"Truthfulness leads to righteousness (*Birr*), and righteousness leads to Paradise."* (Agreed upon).

---
**Teacher Notes:**
*   **Concept Breakdown:** Discuss how honesty goes beyond just "not telling lies." It means being authentic.
*   **Fiqh Literacy Link:** In Islamic law, a single lie can destroy a person's legal credibility. In the Maliki school, a person who is caught lying is classified as having compromised integrity (*Fasiq*) and their testimony in court is rejected.
*   **Interactive Discussion:** *"Is it ever okay to lie to make people laugh?"* Explain that the Prophet (pbuh) warned against lying even when joking: *"Woe to the one who speaks and lies to make the people laugh..."* (Abu Dawud).

---

# Slide 5: Humility (Tawadu'): Defeating the Ego
## Overcoming Pride (Kibr) in the Heart
*   **What is Tawadu'?**
    *   **Tawadu'** (تَوَاضُع) is humility—the state of recognizing that every blessing you have is from Allah, not from your own greatness.
*   **Opposite: Pride (*Kibr* / كِبْر):**
    *   The Prophet (pbuh) defined pride as: *"Rejecting the truth (*Batar al-Haqq*) and looking down on people (*Ghamt al-Nas*)."*
*   **The Spiritual Reality:**
    *   Allah says in the Quran: *"And walk not on the earth with pride. Verily, you cannot rend the earth asunder, nor reach the mountains in height."* (Surah al-Isra: 37).
*   **Prophetic Model:**
    *   The Prophet (pbuh) would repair his own shoes, milk his goats, and serve his family.

---
**Teacher Notes:**
*   **Ash'ari Spiritual Insight:** In Ash'ari spirituality (often taught through the works of classical theologians like Imam al-Ghazali), pride is a fatal sickness of the heart because it assumes that we are independent creators of our success. 
*   **Theology Check:** Remind students: since Allah is the sole Creator of all our talents, wealth, and beauty, boasting about them is intellectually false. We are merely *receivers* of Allah's gifts.
*   **Discussion Starter:** Ask: *"How does humility make a community stronger? How does pride destroy friendships?"*

---

# Slide 6: Controlling Anger: The Power of Hilm
## Forbearance (Hilm) vs. Explosive Rage (Ghadab)
*   **What is Ghadab?**
    *   **Ghadab** (غَضَب) is anger. It is a spark from Shaytan that clouds human intellect (*'Aql*).
*   **The Key Virtues:**
    *   **Kadhm al-Ghaydh** (كَظْم الْغَيْظ): Suppressing rage when you have the power to act on it.
    *   **Hilm** (حِلْم): Forbearance and emotional control—developing a calm, gentle nature over time.
*   **The Prophetic Standard:**
    *   *"The strong person is not the one who can wrestle others down; the strong person is the one who controls himself in moments of anger."* (Muwatta Malik).
*   **Practical Steps to Control Anger:**
    1.  Seek refuge in Allah: Say *A'udhu billahi min ash-Shaytan ir-Rajeem*.
    2.  Change posture: If standing, sit down; if sitting, lie down.
    3.  Perform Wudu: Cool the physical heat of anger with water.

---
**Teacher Notes:**
*   **Textual Focus:** Highlight that Imam Malik placed the Hadith about controlling anger prominently in the *Muwatta*.
*   **Anatomy of Anger:** Explain that anger starts in the heart but manifests in the body. The Sunnah teaches physical hacks (changing posture, Wudu) to disrupt the biological cycle of rage.
*   **Activity:** Have students role-play a scenario where someone insults them. Practice pausing, taking a breath, and responding with *Hilm*.

---

# Slide 7: Creed Connection: Anger, Patience, and Divine Decree
## Connecting Character to Qadar
*   **The Ash'ari View on Qadar (Divine Decree):**
    *   Everything that happens in the universe—both what we like and what we dislike—occurs by Allah's Will (*Iradah*), Knowledge (*'Ilm*), and Power (*Qudrah*).
*   **Anger as Resistance to Decree:**
    *   When we react with explosive anger to accidents, delays, or difficulties, we are, in a spiritual sense, reacting against what Allah has decreed.
*   **Patience (*Sabr*) and Contentment (*Rida*):**
    *   Recognizing that an annoying event (e.g., losing a game, dropping a plate) was decreed by Allah allows us to say: *Qaddara Allahu wa ma sha'a fa'ala* ("Allah has decreed, and what He wills, He does").
    *   This instantly diffuses anger and replaces it with spiritual peace.

---
**Teacher Notes:**
*   **Deepening Belief:** This is a crucial Ash'ari theological application. Connect the sixth pillar of Iman (belief in *Qadar*) directly to everyday emotional control.
*   **Clarification:** Emphasize that accepting *Qadar* does not mean we don't try to fix bad situations. If someone harms us, we seek justice. But we do not lose our inner peace or descend into rage, because we know Allah is in absolute control.
*   **Reflection:** *"How does knowing that an accident was already written in the Preserved Tablet (Al-Lawh al-Mahfudh) make it easier to forgive the person who caused it?"*

---

# Slide 8: Character and the Law: The Concept of Muru'ah
## Nobility and Legal Competency in Maliki Fiqh
*   **What is Muru'ah?**
    *   **Muru'ah** (مُرُوءَة) translates to chivalry, dignity, and honorable behavior.
    *   It means acting in a way that respects local customs, is polite, and avoids foolishness.
*   **The Maliki Legal Link:**
    *   To testify in an Islamic court of law, a witness must have **'Adalah** (عَدَالَة) – upright legal character.
    *   In Maliki fiqh, a person's **'Adalah** is ruined if they lack **Muru'ah**!
*   **What destroys Muru'ah?**
    *   Public tantrums and screaming.
    *   Eating while walking in the street (traditionally considered undignified in classical societies).
    *   Playing foolish pranks, lying for clout, or dressing inappropriately in public.
*   **Ruling:** If you lack *Muru'ah*, your testimony is **rejected** by a Maliki judge (*Qadi*).

---
**Teacher Notes:**
*   **Fiqh Literacy Focus:** This is a unique, powerful concept. Most students think good manners are optional. Show them that in Maliki law, bad character has direct legal consequences.
*   **Historical Context:** Explain that what violates *Muru'ah* can change slightly based on time and place (*'Urf* - custom), but the core principle remains: a Muslim must behave with dignity. 
*   **Discussion:** Ask: *"What are things people do today on social media (like TikTok dances, prank videos) that would destroy their Muru'ah in the eyes of a Maliki judge?"*

---

# Slide 9: Rights of Parents (Birr al-Walidayn)
## The Divine Equation
*   **The Quranic Command:**
    *   Allah says: *"And your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him, and to parents, good treatment."* (Surah al-Isra: 23).
    *   Allah pairs the duty of worshiping Him directly with the duty of honoring parents!
*   **Birr al-Walidayn** (بِرّ الْوَالِدَيْن):
    *   *Birr* is the highest form of active goodness, love, obedience, and respect.
*   **The Ultimate Limit: Say No "Uff":**
    *   Allah forbids even the smallest sigh of frustration (*"Uff"* / أُفّ) toward parents.
*   **What if they command disobedience to Allah?**
    *   We do not obey them in sin, but we must still maintain gentle, kind companionship with them in worldly matters.

---
**Teacher Notes:**
*   **Theological Link:** Point out the sequencing in the Quran. Worship of Allah is the primary right (*Haqq Allah*), and honoring parents is the primary human right (*Haqq al-Adami*).
*   **Obedience Rules:** Clarify that obedience to parents is obligatory (*Wajib*) in everything that is permissible (*Mubah*) or recommended (*Mandub*). It is forbidden to obey them if they command you to leave a clear obligation (like Salah) or commit a sin (like lying).
*   **Vocabulary:** *Birr* (righteousness/extreme goodness) and *Uff* (sound of annoyance).

---

# Slide 10: Legal Rights of Parents in Maliki Law
## Specific Fiqh Rulings
*   **1. Parental Permission for Voluntary Deeds:**
    *   In Maliki fiqh, a child **must** obtain parental permission before embarking on voluntary travel, voluntary military service, or long-term voluntary study away from home if the parents will suffer from their absence.
*   **2. Financial Maintenance (*Nafaqah* / نَفَقَة):**
    *   If parents become poor and cannot support themselves, it is a **strict legal obligation** on their children (who have means) to pay for their food, clothing, housing, and medical care.
*   **3. Testimonial Boundaries:**
    *   In the Maliki school, a child's testimony in court **in favor** of their parents is generally not accepted because of the natural bias of love. However, testifying *against* them is restricted to preserve parent-child honor.

---
**Teacher Notes:**
*   **Fiqh Literacy Details:** Detail the legal nature of *Birr*. It is not just about being polite; it has financial and legal components.
*   **Nafaqah:** Explain that under Islamic law, maintenance (*nafaqah*) is reciprocal. Parents must support young children, and adult children must support elderly, poor parents. This is enforceable by a court.
*   **Discussion:** Why do you think the Maliki school requires parental permission for voluntary travel? (Answer: Because serving parents and keeping their hearts at ease is a higher obligation—*Fard*—than voluntary travels).

---

# Slide 11: Keeping Family Ties (Silat al-Rahim)
## The Sacred Bonds of Kinship
*   **What is Rahim?**
    *   **Rahim** (رَحِم) literally means "womb." 
    *   **Silat al-Rahim** (صِلَة الرَّحِم) means connecting and maintaining relationships with blood relatives (grandparents, siblings, aunts, uncles, cousins).
*   **The Severity of Severing Ties (*Qat' al-Rahim*):**
    *   Severing family ties is a major sin (*Kabirah*).
    *   The Prophet (pbuh) said: *"The severer of family ties will not enter Paradise."* (Agreed upon).
*   **How to maintain ties?**
    *   Visiting them, calling them, sending gifts, helping them financially when they are in need, and forgiving them when they hurt us.
    *   The Prophet (pbuh) said: *"The one who maintains ties is not the one who merely reciprocates. Rather, it is the one who, when his ties are severed, connects them."* (Bukhari).

---
**Teacher Notes:**
*   **Explanation:** Emphasize that *Silat al-Rahim* is not just about visiting relatives who are nice to us. The true test of this virtue is when a relative is distant or rude, and we still make the effort to contact them for the sake of Allah.
*   **Language Tip:** Explain that *Rahim* is derived from Allah's name *Al-Rahman* (The Merciful). The womb represents mercy and connection.
*   **Discussion:** *"How can we maintain family ties with relatives who live far away in other countries?"* (e.g., video calls, sending messages, visiting during holidays).

---

# Slide 12: Rights of Neighbors (Huquq al-Jiwar)
## The Sacred Radius of the Community
*   **The Prophetic Warning:**
    *   The Prophet (pbuh) said: *"Angel Jibril kept advising me to treat neighbors kindly until I thought he would make them my heirs."* (Agreed upon).
*   **Defining the Neighbor in Maliki Fiqh:**
    *   How far does the "neighborhood" go?
    *   **The Maliki Standard:** The neighborhood extends to **forty (40) houses** in every direction (front, back, left, and right).
*   **Core Duties to Neighbors:**
    1.  **Guarding their safety:** Never harming them with noise, smell, or actions.
    2.  **Generosity:** Sharing food, greeting them, and helping them in times of distress.
    3.  **Covering their faults:** Protecting their privacy and dignity.

---
**Teacher Notes:**
*   **The 40-House Rule:** Explain the spatial imagination of Islamic law. It doesn't just mean the person next door; it means the entire local micro-community of 40 houses.
*   **Hadith Check:** Emphasize the strong language of the Prophet (pbuh): *"He is not a believer whose neighbor is not safe from his harm (*Bawa'iq*)."* (Muslim).
*   **Actionable Advice:** Encourage students to think of small acts of kindness: baking cookies for a neighbor, shoveling snow from their walkway, or simply smiling and greeting them.

---

# Slide 13: Property & Neighborhood Rights in Maliki Law
## Specific Legal Safeguards
*   **1. Prevention of Harm (*Da'f al-Darar*):**
    *   In Maliki fiqh, a property owner is **legally blocked** from using their property in a way that causes direct harm to their neighbor.
    *   *Examples:* Building a high wall that blocks the neighbor's sunlight, opening a window that directly overlooks a neighbor's private courtyard, or venting smoke towards their house.
*   **2. Right of Pre-emption (*Shuf'ah* / شُفْعَة):**
    *   If you share property or a common access pathway with a neighbor, and you want to sell your share, you **must offer it to your partner/neighbor first** before selling it to a stranger. 
    *   This prevents unwanted or harmful strangers from encroaching on the neighborhood.

---
**Teacher Notes:**
*   **Fiqh Literacy Focus:** Introduce *Shuf'ah* (Pre-emption). This is a highly developed contract law concept in Maliki fiqh that directly serves social harmony (*Maslahah*).
*   **Darar (Harm):** The Maliki school is very strict on *Darar*. While other schools might say "It's my property, I can build what I want," the Malikis enforce the Prophetic rule: *"There shall be no harming nor reciprocating harm"* (*La darar wa la dirar*).
*   **Application:** If a neighbor complains to a Maliki judge that someone built a window specifically to spy on their women/family, the judge will order the window to be walled up or blocked.

---

# Slide 14: Choosing Companions: The Ethics of Friendship
## The Company You Keep Shapes Your Soul
*   **Suhbah Salihah** (صُحْبَة صَالِحَة): Good, righteous companionship.
*   **The Prophetic Analogy:**
    *   *The Good Friend:* Like a seller of perfume (*Misk*). Even if you don't buy perfume, you leave smelling good.
    *   *The Bad Friend:* Like a blacksmith working a bellows. He either burns your clothes with flying sparks or leaves you smelling like foul smoke.
*   **The Spiritual Influence:**
    *   The Prophet (pbuh) said: *"A person is on the religion of his close friend (*Khalil*), so let each of you look to whom he takes as a close friend."* (Abu Dawud).

---
**Teacher Notes:**
*   **Analysis of the Perfume/Blacksmith Hadith:** Explain that influence is often silent and subconscious. You do not have to copy your friend's bad behavior immediately; just sitting with them regularly causes your heart to become desensitized to sin.
*   **Vocabulary:** *Khalil* (intimate, ultimate friend—a step higher than *Sadiq*).
*   **Discussion:** Ask: *"How do your friends influence the way you talk? The games you play? The way you speak to your parents?"*

---

# Slide 15: Friendship in Court: Maliki Rulings on Witness Testimony
## The Legal Reality of Friendship
*   **The Maliki View on Biased Testimony:**
    *   Islamic law requires witnesses to be completely objective.
    *   In the Maliki school, a person's testimony in court **in favor of their very close friend** (*Shahadat al-Sadiq li-Sadiqihi*) is **rejected**.
*   **Why?**
    *   The legal system recognizes that the bond of close friendship (*Sadaqah*) is so strong that a friend might lie, exaggerate, or overlook the truth out of loyalty to their friend.
*   **The Higher Standard:**
    *   True Islamic friendship does not mean lying for your friend in court. It means helping them stay on the path of truth, even if the truth is against them.

---
**Teacher Notes:**
*   **Fiqh Literacy Concept:** Show the students how the legal reality of friendship is codified in law. In the Maliki school, the judge will ask: *"What is the relationship between the witness and the claimant?"* If they are intimate friends who eat, travel, and share secrets, the testimony is disqualified due to *Tuhmah* (suspicion of bias).
*   **Moral Lesson:** Emphasize that loyalty to Allah and justice (*'Adl*) always comes before loyalty to a friend. 
*   **Hadith Connection:** *"Help your brother whether he is the oppressor or the oppressed."* The Companions asked how to help the oppressor. The Prophet (pbuh) replied: *"By stopping him from oppressing."* (Bukhari).

---

# Slide 16: Confronting Peer Pressure
## Standing Strong in the Face of Fitan (Trials)
*   **What is Peer Pressure?**
    *   The psychological and social force that pushes you to conform to the behavior of those around you to fit in.
*   **Islamic Goal: Guarding the Deen (*Hifdh al-Din*):**
    *   Our primary objective is to protect our faith and relationship with Allah.
*   **Strategies to Resist Peer Pressure:**
    1.  **Define your boundaries early:** If people know you pray and do not lie, they won't ask you to cheat.
    2.  **The power of "No":** Saying "No" is a sign of *Muru'ah* (strength of character) and *Izzah* (honorable pride in Islam).
    3.  **Seek alternative company:** If a group makes you feel bad for practicing your Deen, walk away.

---
**Teacher Notes:**
*   **Pedagogical Discussion:** Peer pressure is one of the biggest challenges for 10-13 year olds. Keep this practical.
*   **Vocabulary:** *Fitan* (plural of *Fitnah* - trials, temptations, confusion).
*   **Scenario Exercise:** Ask students: *"Your friends are laughing at a classmate behind their back and tell you to join in. If you don't, they'll call you a coward. What do you do?"* Discuss how to walk away or change the topic.

---

# Slide 17: Social Media & The Muslim Mindset
## Guarding the Five Necessities (Al-Daruriyyat al-Khams)
*   In Islamic law, the Shariah is designed to protect five essential things: **Religion (*Din*), Life (*Nafs*), Intellect (*'Aql*), Honor/Lineage (*'Ird* / *Nasl*), and Wealth (*Mal*)**.
*   **How does Social Media impact these?**
    *   **Guarding the Mind (*Hifdh al-'Aql*):** Social media algorithms feed addictive, mindless content that wastes time and distracts from deep thought.
    *   **Guarding Honor (*Hifdh al-'Ird* / حِفْظ الْعِرْض):** Social media makes it easy to gossip (*Gheebah*), spread rumors (*Namimah*), spy on others (*Tajassus*), and expose people's private faults.
*   **The Islamic Golden Rule online:**
    *   If you wouldn't say it to someone's face in front of their parents, do not type it online.

---
**Teacher Notes:**
*   **Theological & Legal framework:** Introduce the *Daruriyyat al-Khams* (The Five Necessities) which are the core objectives of the Shariah (*Maqasid al-Shariah*).
*   **Application:** Show how modern technology challenges these ancient legal protections. 
    *   *Honor ('Ird):* Spreading a screenshot of a private chat to humiliate someone is a direct attack on their *'Ird*, which is a major sin in Islam.
    *   *Intellect ('Aql):* Doom-scrolling for hours damages the mind's ability to focus on Salah and Quran.

---

# Slide 18: Blocking the Paths to Harm: Sadd al-Dhara'i'
## A Key Maliki Rule for the Digital Age
*   **What is Sadd al-Dhara'i'?**
    *   **Sadd al-Dhara'i'** (سَدّ الذَّرَائِع) is a famous Maliki legal principle meaning: **"Blocking the means to evil."**
    *   If a permissible action almost always leads to a forbidden result (*Haram*), the Maliki school rules that the action itself becomes restricted or prohibited.
*   **Applying the Principle Online:**
    *   *Example 1:* Following accounts that post inappropriate content. Even if you say "I won't copy them," the path leads to sin. Therefore, you must block/unfollow them (*Sadd al-Dhara'i'*).
    *   *Example 2:* Joining chat groups where cyberbullying or gossiping occurs. The path leads to participating in *Gheebah*. You must leave the group.
*   **Proactive Protection:** We guard our eyes, ears, and hearts before the sin even starts.

---
**Teacher Notes:**
*   **Fiqh Literacy Focus:** Explain the concept of *Sadd al-Dhara'i'* clearly. It is one of the defining features of Maliki jurisprudence. While some schools look only at the final act, Imam Malik looked at the pathways that lead to the act.
*   **Interactive Challenge:** Ask the class: *"What is an app or feature on your phone that you had to delete or turn off because it kept leading you to waste time or see bad things?"* Explain that this action of deleting it is a practical application of *Sadd al-Dhara'i'*.

---

# Slide 19: Justice ('Adl) and Equity (Qist)
## The Universal Scales of Islam
*   **What is 'Adl?**
    *   **'Adl** (عَدْل) means justice, putting everything in its proper place, and giving everyone their due right.
*   **What is Qist?**
    *   **Qist** (قِسْط) is equity—ensuring fairness in practical distribution and treatment, taking into account individual circumstances.
*   **The Command to be Just to All:**
    *   Allah says: *"O you who believe! Stand out firmly for justice, as witnesses to Allah, even though it be against yourselves, or your parents, or your kin..."* (Surah an-Nisa: 135).
*   **Opposite: Oppression (*Zulm* / ظُلْم):**
    *   Allah says in a Hadith Qudsi: *"O My servants! I have forbidden oppression (*Zulm*) for Myself, and I have made it forbidden among you, so do not oppress one another."* (Muslim).

---
**Teacher Notes:**
*   **Vocabulary Differentiation:** Clarify the nuance between *'Adl* (strict justice/equality under the law) and *Qist* (distributive equity/fairness that accounts for differences). 
*   **Illustration:** If you have two siblings—one is 5 years old and the other is 15 years old—giving them both the exact same shoe size is "equal" but unjust. Giving them sizes that fit them is *Qist*.
*   **Crucial Creed Detail:** In Ash'ari theology, Allah is Al-'Adl. Because He is the absolute owner of creation, whatever He does is just by definition. Oppression (*Zulm*) is impossible for Allah because oppression means violating someone else's rights, and everything belongs to Allah.

---

# Slide 20: The Common Good: Maslahah Mursalah
## Using Maliki Legal Principles to Treat Others Well
*   **What is Maslahah Mursalah?**
    *   **Maslahah Mursalah** (مَصْلَحَة مُرْسَلَة) is a Maliki legal source meaning: **"Unrestricted Public Interest."**
    *   It refers to creating rules or taking actions that bring benefit or prevent harm to society, even if there is no specific Quranic text about that exact issue.
*   **Living the Principle:**
    *   How do we treat others well using *Maslahah*?
    *   *Example 1: Traffic Rules.* Stopping at red lights is not in the Quran, but it protects human life (*Maslahah*). We obey it as a religious duty.
    *   *Example 2: School Rules.* Keeping the classroom clean, not using phones during class, and recycling are actions that build a healthy environment for everyone.
*   **Being a force for good:** A Muslim is always looking for ways to benefit the community.

---
**Teacher Notes:**
*   **Fiqh Literacy Focus:** *Maslahah Mursalah* is another pillar of Maliki legal methodology (*Usul al-Fiqh*). Explain that Imam Malik was famous for using this principle to address new social problems.
*   **Connection to Character:** Show that a good Muslim doesn't just ask, *"Is there a specific rule forcing me to do this?"* Instead, they ask, *"Does this action help my community and please Allah?"*
*   **Discussion:** Ask: *"Can you think of a modern rule in your town or school that helps everyone, even though it wasn't around 1400 years ago?"* (e.g., speed limits, internet safety rules).

---

# Slide 21: Sources and Bibliography
## Building on Classical Foundations
*   **Primary Fiqh Texts:**
    *   Imam Malik ibn Anas, *Al-Muwatta* (Collection of Hadith and legal practice of Madinah).
    *   Ibn Abi Zayd al-Qayrawani, *Al-Risalah* (The classical Maliki manual of law).
    *   Al-Hattab al-Maliki, *Mawahib al-Jalil* (Comprehensive commentary on Maliki fiqh).
*   **Primary Creed & Akhlaq Texts:**
    *   Imam al-Sanusi, *Al-Aqidah al-Sanusiyyah* (Standard Ash'ari creed).
    *   Imam al-Ghazali, *Ihya 'Ulum al-Din* (Revival of the Religious Sciences - Akhlaq section).
    *   Imam al-Qarafi, *Al-Furuq* (Maliki legal distinctions and public interest philosophy).
*   **Modern Fiqh Literacy Reference:**
    *   Shaykh Muhyiddin ibn 'Arabi (and other commentators on the *Risalah* of Al-Qayrawani).

---
**Teacher Notes:**
*   **Closing Remarks:** Encourage students to appreciate that the rules of character, social media, and family rights are not arbitrary. They are built on the deep, intellectual inheritance of the Maliki and Ash'ari schools.
*   **Review:** Do a quick verbal quiz on the terms learned: *Sidq*, *Tawadu'*, *Muru'ah*, *Shuf'ah*, *Sadd al-Dhara'i'*, *Maslahah Mursalah*.

# Slide 1: Welcome & Course Overview
## Character, Society & Family: The Outer Mirror of the Inner Soul

*   **Key Themes:**
    *   Honesty, Humility, and Anger Management (*Sidq*, *Tawadu'*, *Kadhm al-Ghaydh*)
    *   Rights of Parents, Family, and Neighbors (*Birr al-Walidayn*, *Silat al-Rahim*, *Huquq al-Jiwar*)
    *   Choosing Friends and Navigating Peer Pressure (*Suhbah Salihah*)
    *   Social Media Ethics: Protecting Deen, Mind, and Honor
    *   Justice, Public Interest, and Legal Chivalry (*'Adl*, *Maslahah*, *Muru'ah*)

---
**Teacher Notes:**
*   **Welcome & Objective:** Welcome the students. Explain that this unit transitions from individual worship (*Taharah* and *Salah*) to social responsibility (*Mu'amalat*) and character development (*Akhlaq*).
*   **Pedagogical Note:** Highlight that we are studying these topics through the systematic framework of the **Maliki school of law** and the **Ash'ari school of creed**. Explain that character in Islam is not just an optional set of nice behaviors; it is deeply connected to theological truths and legal obligations.
*   **Discussion Starter:** Ask: *"Can a person have a perfect prayer (Salah) if they go home and treat their parents or neighbors poorly? Why is there a connection between worship and character?"*
